In 1928, the government of the United Kingdom lent H.M.C. ships "Champlain" and "Vancouver" to the Canadian government; since that time, these ships have formed part of the Royal Canadian Navy. The government of the United Kingdom decided that these ships, by reason of age and deterioration, were to be rendered ineffective as ships of war, as of December 31, 1936, in accordance with the terms of the London Naval Treaty of 1930. H.M.C. ships "Champlain" and "Vancouver" have been demilitarized and, it is expected, will shortly be disposed of in Canada on behalf of the government of the United Kingdom.
It being necessary to replace "Champlain" and "Vancouver," the problem received very careful consideration, and, on ascertaining that it would take too long to build ships in Canada or elsewhere, negotiations towards finding replacements from the Royal Navy were commenced in 1936.
The price finally agreed upon is $1,000,000 per ship, including armament and stores. The replacements will be named H.M.C. ships "Fraser" and "St. Laurent," and will be commissioned in the Royal Canadian Navy within the next few weeks.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTROL OF ATHLETICS AND PHYSICAL AND RECREATIONAL TRAINING
PROPOSED CONTROL OF ATHLETICS AND PHYSICAL AND RECREATIONAL TRAINING
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, in the interests of public health there should be established a ministry of sports.
He said: Mr. Speaker, since giving notice of this resolution I have revised my opinion as to its wording, to the extent that if the resolution were to propose that the control of athletics and of physical training in this country be a branch only of, say, the Department of Pensions and National Health,

"f my general purposes would be served. I am mot seeking an amendment to the resolution as it now stands, however, for the reason that Rich an amendment would not alter or affect the general purport of my remarks.
For reasons which I shall submit, Mr. Speaker, I consider that the time is ripe for this government to consider the advisability of assuming control of athletics and physical and recreational training in this country on a national basis consistent with the constitutional authority therefor, and otherwise to cooperate with the provincial governments in a like scheme. Obviously the matter of a nation's health is of the greatest importance, and this question has commanded the attention of some of the leading countries in Europe and Asia. In France there is actually a ministry of sports. In Czechoslovakia there is a highly organized branch of the government which for some years past has been devoted to a national scheme of physical training, and I assume it is more than general knowledge that similar systems are in force in Germany, Russia and Japan. What is more significant still, however, and what I think will be of greater interest to the members of this house, is the fact that in the speech from the throne at the recent opening of the British house this very subject was given special prominence. I happened to be present at debates in both houses when the matter was debated extensively, or, if I may so describe it, when the nation's ill health was discussed at some length. Logically enough, the subject was closely identified with athletics and physical training in all its branches.
I mention this because it is my considered opinion that Great Britain and the other European countries which I have just named are keeping pace with the fast changing conditions in the world's economic and social life by adopting legislation such as is proposed by this resolution. Further, it is my opinion that it is high time for this government to consider the adoption of some national scheme of physical training for the people of this country.
Let us examine our local situation as it exists in Canada to-day. It is true that as Canadians we are a people who have been reared with an athletic background. Two of our Canadian games-I refer to hockey and lacrosse-are now international in their scope and are played in most of the leading countries of Europe. That this is so to my mind indicates two things. One is the active world interest that is now displayed in physical training; the second is the sporting atmosphere in which we Canadians have been

Public Health-Mr. Plaxton
reared. I mention that for this reason, that any scheme which contemplates the improvement of the health of the people of this country on a national basis necessarily must be associated with athletics in all its branches, and to that extent, consistent again with the constitutional authority that may exist, we must assume control of athletics in this country.
This brings me to a consideration of our local problem with regard to amateur sports. In Canada to-day the control of amateur sports has been appropriated by groups or associations, self-constituted in their authority, which generally speaking owe allegiance to no one, and which within the confines of their particular sports are virtually dictators, even as to the locality in which the sports may be carried on. The result, I submit, is chaotic if we are to look for any attempt on the part of those associations to cooperate not only between themselves but with the public and the governments of this country. Likewise it may be said of amateurism that several of the prominent gate-producing games-that is, games which the public pay money to see- have developed into something of a racket as far as the contestants and the managements are concerned. I must add, however, that the situation in this regard is not too alarming, and that it could be cleaned up by legislation such as is proposed by this resolution. But I must reaffirm this statement, that any scheme for improving the health of the people on a national basis, involving physical and recreational training, necessarily involves a control of athletics. I can qualify that statement by saying I would not contemplate the exercise of such control with respect to particular sports except in so far as it may be deemed necessary to the furtherance of the general scheme.
There is one phase of amateurism with regard to which I must make some comment. I refer to Olympic games and other international contests. One has only to recall the lamentable showing of our Olympic representatives at the games last year, and particularly the fiasco involving our hockey team, with all the well deserved, well merited unfavourable criticism that the games inspired, to realize the force of my remarks. Consider the methods by which the contestants were chosen, the sectionalism displayed in that connection, the action of those in charge both in Canada and abroad, the almost total failure of our representatives to win anything, and finally, the crowning blow, the losing of our hockey title-and all this, mind you, at a considerable cost to the taxpayers
31111-8i
of this country. Need I say more, sir, to convince hon. members of this house that the time is long past when any athlete or group of athletes who presume to represent Canada in Canada's name should be permitted to do so in any international contest without proper supervision and control by someone responsible to this government.
In opposition to this proposal someone may bring up that old catch word "regimentation." In that connection I may say that in our provincial system of education one finds the perfect example of regimentation. The cry may be raised: "Do not regiment the young people of this country into a measure of physical fitness." Well, I submit that argument is untenable and inconsistent, and I will leave it at that. Others may advance as an argument the catch word "cannon fodder." They seem to feel that there is in this proposal a sinister attempt to establish a scheme to permit peace time military training of the young men of this country. My answer to that is that if the question of the defence of this country should ever arise, it would be preferable to have an army in the highest state of physical fitness rather than one of which the reverse is true. Likewise, is it reasonable to say that because we are training the young men of this country to a high standard of physical fitness they are necessarily being trained for war or will necessarily go to war?
Finally the problem boils down to one of the nation's health. I do not intend to burden the house with facts and figures in that connection. Some people may say, we are a healthy race; why worry? Perhaps that is so. but let me point to a startling discovery which the British authorities made in recent months. I find in a long editorial which I clipped from the London Times of November 12 last dealing with the nation's physique a few statements which I think will be of interest to the house. The opening paragraph reads:
The policy of improving the nation's physique, as foreshadowed in the king's speech, seems to have captured the popular imagination to a remarkable degree. Both houses of parliament have made it one of the main features of the first debates of the new session, and many authoritative correspondents in these columns have made constructive suggestions for perfecting a project of which they all approve.
Then further down:
The second fact brought out in debates and in correspondence is the existence of a general agreement that the present standard of the national physique is far from satisfactory.

Public Health-Mr. Graydon
And a third statement is:
In the case of the city slum some fifty years of partisan pondering failed to effect the cure which five years of united national effort is now certain to provide. In the case of the body slum it is natural that success should come more slowly; but it will come beyond a doubt if it is fostered by the same spirit.
Yes, we might be shocked if we saw a true picture of this country's condition as far as health is concerned. One need only look at the hundreds of hospitals and sanatoria full to the roof to make us apprehensive of the true condition. Then we must also realize that thousands of our fellow Canadians during the last six or seven years have been obliged to live on relief and in idleness. That situation to my own personal knowledge, particularly in urban centres, has induced considerable ill health amongst those unfortunates.
In the final analysis however the situation can be summed up by stating that whatever the present conditions may be in regard to the health of the nation, they can be improved vastly by the adoption of a national scheme of physical training, rather than continuing the haphazard state of things which now prevails.
I have not attempted to exhaust this subject. The resolution in its present form is perhaps not a practicable one, but I hope I have dealt with the matter at sufficient length to commend its general principle to the earnest and serious consideration of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I desire in joining in the debate on this resolution first to comment on the qualifications, which I think must be obvious to all in the house, of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) to deal with matters of sport. They are well known to all who come from that section of Ontario, or for that matter, anywhere in the Dominion of Canada.
I congratulate the proposer of this resolution not only upon having brought to the attention of the house the matter of public health and sport, but also upon the experience .and knowledge which he has with relation thereto.
As the hon. member who proposed the resolution so aptly said, two of the great international sports with which Canada is particularly identified are hockey and lacrosse. Xacrosse, we all know, has been regarded for many years as Canada's national game. When William Perkins Bull, K.C., the historian of the county of Peel, wrote a year or more ago a delightful volume entitled Prom Rattlesnake Hunt to Hockey, he referred to the town of Brampton, the county town of Peel,

as the cradle and nursery of that great game. It is therefore with particular pleasure that I take part in this debate. In addition I might point out that the county of Peel has the same name as the great Cumberland huntsman John Peel, whose name is familiar in poetry and song.
In the year 1914 the lacrosse club of Brampton took a forward step in going to Vancouver to challenge and do battle with the Vancouver lacrosse team for the championship of the world. Defeated by a narrow margin then, they challenged again in 1930 and defeated the New Westminster club, winning the highest honours in the world of lacrosse. Since that time of course a change has occurred in that great game; instead of having a twelve-man game we now have box lacrosse. That perhaps is not nationally so well known, but in my county night after night throughout the spring, summer and fall, large numbers of Peel people are not only spectators of the game but actually participate in it. Many in the house will recall the great battles which have taken place in the past between the Brampton Excelsiors and teams from Orangeville, Weston, St. Catharines and towns in the vicinity of Toronto and elsewhere. These are things which come back to the memories of many hon. members, and bring to our attention the importance of this sport in our national life. I would also be remiss if, bearing the name of Graydon, I did not make some mention of the old Toronto Tecumsehs, who' in years gone by, with the Nationals of Montreal and the Torontos, staged so many great battles for the lacrosse crown of that time.
In considering the many types of physical training and the advancements which have been made in methods of fostering the health of our citizens, we should not forget to mention the great work being done throughout the dominion by the Young Men's Christian Association. That organization is doing an effective job in promoting better health and providing facilities for exercise and recreation for our young people. I think the government should encourage such organizations.
The service clubs are not far behind in the promotion of good health. In our own town of Brampton the Lions Club has done splendid work in a centre where there has always been much activity in connection with sports. This summer they were able to finance a swimming pool which will be constructed in the Swinburne memorial park.
The hon. member for Trinity has referred to the importance of the health of our people and I suggest to the Minister of Pensions and

Public Health-Mr. Mclvor
National Health (.Mr. Power) that the matter of medical examination is also very important. As was stated in the debate last night, a number of insurance companies are already conducting intensive surveys among their policyholders in this connection. I would not be living to-day were it not for the fact that when I was much younger I had a medical examination which revealed a weakness which after some time was successfully corrected. For that reason, among others, I have a special interest in this matter. The hon. member for Trinity has suggested the systematic training of our people, but I would consider it no less important that we should have as well a proper inventory of our resources of physical health.
If the Minister of Pensions and National Health will give careful and studied attention to the matter which has been brought up this afternoon I feel sure that more of our people will be given the opportunity and encouragement to play at healthful sport from time to time. I can speak from personal experience of the need of such a move, because I am one of those who do not take sufficient exercise. To-day we do not seem to have the time to exercise. There is the keen competition in business and the fact that we use our cars so much. Some will almost use a car to go from Wellington street to the Peace Tower. Such practices are devastating to our individual constitutions and have an adverse effect upon our national life. In certain centres of this dominion we find many thousands of people watching no more than twenty men put on a performance in one of our national games. That would not be so bad if we could or would walk to see the games, but sometimes we simply sit in our living room and listen to the radio and get no exercise at all. These are things that should be brought to the attention of the people of Canada, because they have a very important bearing upon our national wellbeing. As the hon. member for Trinity has said, we are a hardy people and with our healthful climate there is no reason why we should not hold a very high place in every sport that is played.
I am glad to note that the hon. member has not carried out his original proposal that a ministry of sports should be established. I do not think the present position of the taxpayers of Canada would permit that move being taken at this time. I think the hon. member's motion has been worth while even if it does nothing more than draw the attention of the government and the people of Canada to a very important matter with
respect to our national health. If the very impressionable Minister of Pensions and National Health is able to work out something whereby he can provide additional facilities and encouragement along this line, we shall' at least have made an auspicious start in a. work which I believe to be most important to the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate because I am still a youth. I have played at most of the games that are played in Canada, and I have received great benefits from such participation. I congratulate the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) upon bringing this matter before parliament. Anything that concerns the use of leisure time is of great importance to our citizens. We have an eight hour day in organized labour and I expect that that will soon be cut down to a six hour or perhaps a four hour day. We are then faced with the question of whether this leisure time will be spent in places of a questionable nature or out in the open air.
I should like to quote a great athlete of days long gone by. St. Paul said that it is absolutely necessary for us to keep our bodies in shape. Many of our youths are taking part in athletics. I should like to give an instance of some junior hockey players in that noted centre of sport, Fort William. Two players, Bill Grant and "Fire" Parsons were coming home from a hockey game. They were on their way to have lunch when they found a pocket-book containing $81 in cash, some cheques and other things. Instead of going to have their lunch these two young men walked to the other end of the city to give the owner back his money. That sort of thing on the part of our youth is nothing less than heroism. Many of our boys get their names into the papers for other reasons, but when they show themselves to be absolutely honest it gives great promise and hope for the future of our youth. I happen to be the chaplain of that team and I am happy to be able to report that there is not a smoker on the team.
The benefits which come from outdoor sports are quite evident. Last year when I urged the leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) to assist us in having a little recreation, both of these old time athletes stated their willingness to do the best they could. I feel sure that the mover of this resolution is going to have splendid support. We must remember that those who.
Public Health-Mr. Church

take part in games learn to keep their tempers; they learn to have definite aims, and they learn to come back when they are beaten.
I think the resolution in its present form is well worthy of consideration. Our athletes should be placed in a position where those of them who are not able to buy a hockey stick or a pair of skates should be assisted and encouraged. Many of us are limited in our means but our country is not limited, and I believe that one of the outstanding arguments in favour of this motion is the necessity. now that we have so much leisure on our hands, of training our youth in sports and physical exercise, and as well our middle-aged and some of our older people who need to work off fat into bone and muscle and brain energy.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) has brought up this question. He has not brought it up in exactly the way he first proposed, and as was announced in the sporting press of the country. His first proposal was that we should have an athletic commission with jurisdiction over amateur and professional sport all over Canada. That was announced in the press, and it was not favoured by the sporting editors of the country inasmuch as this parliament would have no jurisdiction, property and civil rights being a matter for the provinces.
The hon. member for Trinity is an active sportsman. He was a member of the Varsity hockey team that went out to Vancouver and brought back the Allan cup in 192/ and was a splendid type of sportsman. When he came to me and talked this matter over early last session, because I had a motion before the house with respect to national health and physical welfare, I told him that I would gladly give way to him because I knew he was a sportsman. But he did not have the right idea about this question at that time. We talked the matter over and he told me that he would bring it up in a bill last session. It was not on the present lines and had no relation to health.
Last year I drew to the attention of the house the friction over sending Olympic teams to the old country, which was causing a great deal of international discord. At that time a big row was in progress over sending our hockey team from Moncton over to the Olympic games. It was a very fine team, and because I considered that the maritimes got a very raw deal from the hockey authori-

ties I brought the matter before the house. Let me give the house a few of the headlines that appeared in the press at that time:
British and U.S. officials engage in heated argument-Olympic committee finally lifts ban on Canadian players on English team at request of Canada. Dominion and old country will meet to-morrow.
This is another heading:
C.A.H.A. president, E. A. Gilroy, charges overseas hockey is "racket"-Dissension revolving around the eligibility of two English hockey players is renewed with mounting bitterness, and four European teams are ready to protest England's victories because of Foster and Archer. Second gold medal to Germany.
Again:
Canada ready quit Olympic hockey games. Claim play-off system will put team at disadvantage. New bombshell hits tournament.
Maple leaf squad will withdraw unless rule is rescinded.
These are all headlines on dispatches from the front. This is another one:
Olympic boys very peeved. Hand out blasts against officials in charge of team.
Such were the dispatches that came from the Olympic hockey games last year, and undoubtedly it caused a great deal of friction in the old country and in the British Empire.
As I said, the hon. member for Trinity wanted, first of all, to have an athletic commission with jurisdiction over amateur and professional sport all over Canada, but that would not have been within the jurisdiction of this parliament. I urged upon this house last year that it would be far better to stay out of the Olympic games because there was nothing but rows before our teams went over, rows when they got over there, and rows when they returned. It caused a great deal of international bitterness, and it would have been far better for us to eliminate the Olympics and stick to the British Empire games. There is, in my opinion, very little sport for sport's sake in the Olympic games.
I had a resolution on the order paper of March 31 of 1936 reading as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, a select or other committee of the house should be appointed to consider and report on making recreation and sport a national branch of government. and of the state under the Minister of Health, to not only promote national health and the physical welfare of the people, but also with a view to the upbuilding of a more healthy race, to aid them to better meet the many social changes of the age, and to promote good citizenship, in conjunction with provincial and municipal authority.
Subsequently, after the hon. member for Trinity came to me and talked the matter over, I told him that it would be all right with me for him to take over this matter

Public Health-Mr. Church
and bring it before the house. As far as the resolution now before the house goes, it refers, and quite properly, to health, and in that connection I wish to quote from two eminent authorities. Lord Dawson of Penn recently warned the students of Guy's Hospital Medical School of our progress towards national suicide. He said:
The problem of rearing a fit race transcends in importance all other domestic questions. By the improvement of medical knowledge and by the quickening of the public conscience, we have cut down the death-rate and thereby-enabled to survive many unfit people whom in the old days nature eliminated. This bad stock is a dead-weight on the nation. These people are passengers in the national omnibus, and if they propagate, which they do not hesitate to do, the damage they inflict is carried on to future generations. No policy which aims at raising the national physique can succeed if it does not take cognizance of these biological facts.
Our piecemeal social policy has no coherent purpose, and is too much shaped by expediency. There is not behind it the study of scientific law and biological facts on which alone the health of a people can be founded. Palling death-rates are only matters for congratulation in proportion as they denote the preservation of people healthy enough to enjoy life and effective enough to be sound workers and sound players.
That was from the king's physician. This is what Lord Horder, one of the most eminent physicians in the world, says as to the necessity of health:
A national stock-taking shows some unpalatable facts. In this country, one in 120 persons is feeble-minded, one in 200 is insane, one in 10 is too dull or too sickly to be absorbed into industry. The expense of educating and caring for these inefficients is enormous, but more serious is the fact that the future stock is being recruited from them.
The writer of the article from which I am quoting goes on to say in the English Review, December, 1936:
We were warned also in 1934 by Sir George Newman, then Chief Medical Officer to the Board of Education, who wrote in his annual report on the health of the school-child: "The exceptional saving of infant life since 1910 has added to the population thousands of young children who under different circumstances would not have survived. If we are saving as many physically and mentally enfeebled children, it is obvious that we must anticipate a heavy burden of defective children in the schools at five years of age. . . . When we come to observe 100 children of the age of twelve years in an average elementary school, we shall find that 75 per cent of them reveal more or less serious defects."
The writer of the article goes on to say:
These terrible words, coming from men who command the greatest respect and authority, must force us, unless we are consciously and deliberately bent on national decay, to revise not merely our ideas about the so-called social services but the very foundations of our morality.
These are the opinions of two of the most eminent medical men in the world.
While I shall speak for only five or six minutes longer, I want to take time to pay tribute to our Minister of National Health (Mr. Power). He is an old sportsman; he commanded a Toronto company at the front, and he is respected in that city by the rank and file of soldiers and sportsmen. He is also an old hockey player. Like the hon. member for Trinity, I have every confidence that the minister will take up this matter of public importance and others which deserve careful consideration by this house.
Anglo-Saxons are a sporting race. As has been said, on the green fields of Eton Waterloo was won; and the first duty of a government is to look after the health, peace, prosperity and welfare of its people. In the motherland, Mr. Speaker, they take part in sport the way you used to do. One might say that everybody there is a sportsman. The men, women and children of England have been bom and bred in a love of outdoor life, though it may be only walking, or cross country riding, or some similar exercise. They are not content to be mere spectators. The whole British Empire has followed their example, with the result that it has commanded the admiration and respect of the world. To-day England is recovering because of the health of her people, fostered by their love of sport; she is leading the world in many ways, such as in balanced budgets, in tariffs, in recreational schemes, in reconstruction, and to promote recovery, she has also a housing policy, which, as the Minister of National Health mentioned last night, is a most important matter, related to public health.
A country does not belong solely to those who live in it to-day; it is an inheritance from the past; it is a possession for the present, and a trust for the future. As far as our country is concerned I would pay tribute to the Ontario high school, public school and separate school coaching teachers in sport who are taking care of the children after hours, doing volunteer work to develop the physique of our future citizens. I was sorry to see cadet training abolished, because it had a great influence on public health; it led to respect for authority, discipline and manliness; it was, as I see it, not a military organization, but a means of physical development. Many of our people are beneficiaries of that system; it has the support of reliable medical authority, and it has done good work in Ontario.
Public Health-Mr. Church

When I was on the board of education there was a considerable need of public playgrounds in Toronto. We got an intercollegiate union formed of the public schools and the high schools. When I became controller there was hardly a civic playground in Toronto except Moss Park and the Osier playground. We took over those two playgrounds and we made the work part of the parks department. The public parks then were run largely on the principle of "keep off the grass" and that sort of thing; thousands of dollars were spent, and nobody could play in some of the parks. That system was changed. The greatest asset of such a department, as I see it, is the recreational feature, not only for the sake of the school children but also for use for playing games after working hours, in connection with daylight saving, in industrial districts.
This is a work in which the press could help if it would, but of late years three-fourths of the space in the newspapers has been devoted to professional sport. After all, the amateur plays the game for the love of it, to win it if he can in a fair way before the eyes of all men. I am not opposed to professional sport if it is well conducted. I believe that it is the duty of this parliament- because there is concurrent jurisdiction between the dominion and the provinces in connection with education, health and many other matters-to do something, through the Minister of National Health, along the lines of this resolution. The late Doctor Hastings, a great medical officer who became known over the whole of North America through his battle for public health, was very strongly of that opinion. I hope that before long the federal Minister of National Health will put into effect a policy of making grants for this purpose. I would not give these grants to the provinces, because they would put it into their pockets for provincial purposes. These grants should be paid to the boards of education, the high school, separate school and public school boards and municipalities of the country, through a federal commission or subcommittee appointed by the minister, with the object of developing the physical condition of the youth of the land by direct federal aid. Military training is practically abolished, even from our city schools in Toronto. We have a great many doctors on the Toronto board of education. Some are distinguished medical men and dentists, but others are rather like honorary colonels; they are doctors of all kinds, doctors of theology, music, law and pedagogy; in fact anybody who is a trustee and cannot call himself a doctor had

better qualify by the next meeting. However, we have a most progressive board of education of good men in Toronto, one second to none in the dominion. They give a great deal of time voluntarily to their work, but I may add that while I did not agree with their action in abolishing the cadet training, they are doing the finest work in education.
I have said that the press in the sporting pages could help, but for the last few years it has paid very little attention to amateur sport. You do not see much about university and high school participation in sports, but you can read pages of stuff about " pro " sport in its various forms. I am not opposed to professional sport when properly conducted; the public believe in it, and it has come to be a necessity. But I do contend that we should have a national policy of recreation and games, not only in respect of playgrounds, as I have indicated, but also to promote a national parks system that will develop our outdoor life as the British people are doing in the British isles. The government owns large tracts of land. It has practically no federal park in Ontario, which can be linked up to Trent lake, Simcoe, Georgian bay, Muskoka and right to the Lake of Bays and Algonquin park. The dominion owns a great deal of land, and a fine people's playground for the province could be created; it would benefit the hospitals and help develop the youth of the land. A similar scheme could be adopted in all the other provinces.
In conclusion, as regards these Olympic games, I am not in favour of any more grants to them, for I think they do more harm than good. There are too many governing bodies in sport, and too many concerned with it who are not connected with any club at all. Olympic games are held each five years; then they subside, and you hear nothing about them until another comes along.
Where is our national game, lacrosse, to-day? It can revive itself; it does not need any reviving. It is a sport that used to be followed in the schools, and is yet played in Toronto.
With regard to cricket, a great deal of good was done by the visit to the old country of the Canadian team, and the credit is due to a former member of this house. The game of cricket is one of the few remaining games which at this time has not been professionalized.
I suggest that a committee of the house might collect information along public health lines, and might consult with boards of education, boards of health and other provincial

Public Health-Mr. Church
bodies in an effort to find out what should be done. There can be no doubt that in the years to come the physical development of our youth will be one of our most important problems. That point is brought out by Lord Dawson of Penn and Lord Horder.
A few days ago I was reading an article written by a German, educationist. I believe the gentleman in question has written a book which is available in the library, English Review, December, 1986, new book review. In his observations he referred to the decadence of the British race. He says that one Englishman is an idiot, two are a football game and three are the British Empire. Another German author has said that where there is one Englishman, there is the British Empire. We have to take our hats off to old John Bull, and must respect the way he plays the game. We know he plays it for the love of it, and before the eyes of all men.
When I was a member of the board of health for the city of Toronto, Doctor Hastings came into the life of our city, and it was at that time we made our playgrounds the finest on the continent. We know that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, and especially is that true among the youth of our land.
The youth of Canada are a credit to the country, notwithstanding the depression and the hard times through which the fathers who are sending them to school have had to pass. Many of those fathers have had to sacrifice some of the necessities of life in order to be able to send their children to school. The parents of the children in our schools are among the finest sportsmen in the dominion, and I hope the time is not far distant when Canada may have a proper national health department,-not a skeleton department locked up in a cupboard like Old Mother Hubbard's. I am not for one moment reflecting on the splendid deputy and' assisting officers in the minister's department. I have known them all my life and have reason to believe that they are able physicians and educated men who stand most high in ability in their profession. Nevertheless I should like to see these officers supported in a national department which would be a real department of health and which would consider different methods of bringing about better health among our people. We realize that this is one of the most important problems we have to face as a people.
I suggest the minister might well consider the matter which has been placed before him by the hon. member for Trinity. A committee could be appointed to go into the matter of national public health, and should
be instructed to develop a proper public health department. We know this work has been left on the shoulders of the municipalities. The city of Toronto has developed a great department which has cost the taxpayers a large sum of money, but the results have been excellent. When the department was originated we had none of the modern means of preserving public health, such as those to which the minister referred last night. Milk has to be inspected, and special precautions are necessary in connection with food and other matters. Although the officers who preceded Doctor Hastings were all most excellent men, with the help they got, yet it was Doctor Hastings who developed the modern health department of Toronto and expanded it. As the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said last night, much of the health research work is now done by the universities, private philanthropists and municipalities. But the municipalities will have to place the burden on real estate, and real estate can stand the burden no longer.
Life is not worth living unless there is health. No matter how much money a person has, he is poor unless he has health. To-day the government is spending $2,000,000 on the health of animals, but only $500,000 on the health in Canada of ten million individuals. I say the municipality must be relieved of some of the real estate burdens. If we are to develop the hardy race to which reference was made by the two gentlemen to whom I have referred, we must have help from parliament given to the municipalities in connection with public health.
Last night we heard a good speech from the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann), and with his observations I fully agree. Out of all the moneys that are being collected through taxation, do hon. members know how much the city of Toronto will receive? Well, from the main estimates we are to have $17,000 to be spent on the eastern gap, and a few extra dollars for revolving doors and other repairs on the post office, or a total of $20,000. That is what the city of Toronto, in which there are Liberals as well as Conservatives, is to receive, and the federal government get $90,000,000 in revenue from that city.
In Toronto we maintain a first class life saving station, and at times we have to send our crews as far as Georgian bay and other outlaying sections, all at the expense of the Toronto taxpayer. In the time of Doctor Hastings we were able to make progress in

Public Health-Mr. Douglas
health measures because there was a city income tax, as an exclusive field from 1867 to the municipalities. Then the dominion authorities came into the field. Public health costs money, and I say the municipalities and real estate cannot carry the burden any longer. Boards of education cannot do it. We must have some support from the federal department of health.
The minister, I believe, would do well if he could see his way clear to read into the resolution what was suggested last March in something I had placed on the order paper. I believe a committee of this house or of both houses should consider the matter of national public health in all its phases, as it has been done in England. Many of our families have been seriously injured by the depression, and because of it some are on relief. Despite their difficulties, however, we must admire the way our industrial workers have carried on in sending their children to the high schools of Toronto. I believe parliament would be doing them a good turn if it were to appoint such a committee as I suggested last March.

Mr. Speaker, I shall require only a few moments to place before the house the views of the group to which I belong. First of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) upon bringing this matter to the attention of parliament. It is an old saying that the battle of Waterloo was won on the playgrounds of England. It is true that many of the battles of life are won on our playgrounds.
I am intensely interested in sport, and I should like hon. members to understand that anything I may say is not said because of a lack of appreciation of sport but rather because of a recognition of the part sport, in conjunction with other factors, must play in the building of our national life. First of all may I say I am glad the mover changed the motion so as not to ask for a ministry of sport. In the amended motion he asks only that the Department of Pensions and National Health shall incorporate the ideas he has put forth into its work of enhancing the health of our people.
There are two points I suggest we ought to bear in mind: First, to a great extent the matter of health and the development of sport and recreation is in the provincial field, and the physical training mentioned by the mover is carried on chiefly by the provincial education and health departments. Further, to a great extent sport is supervised by provincial

athletic organizations. To set up now a national body that would tend to overlap would be simply to infringe upon another field. Of course the Department of National Defence sets aside a certain amount of money for cadet training. If the government would consider the feasibility of spending that money for the development of athletic clubs I for one believe it would go further in promoting the general health of our people than it goes as we are now spending it. I do not think a sports ministry, or even to have the Department of Pensions and National Health handle a national program, would be feasible. I believe the question of sports is largely a provincial matter, and one that should be handled by the provincial departments of education and health.
I do think there may be a place for a commission on cultural development, which might seek to promulgate national drama, national musical festivals and some type of national recreation. But when we come to consider the feasibility of spending a sum of money on a sports ministry, or even a sub-department of sports under the minister of health, it seems to me there are one or two other things that should be considered also, not because sport is less important but because there are some other things that are far more important. I grant you, Mr. Speaker, that sport and recreation do make for healthy bodies, but there are other things that are more important than recreation. Some of them are preventive dentistry; the proper care of children, particularly infants, and a proper program of mental and physical hygiene. At the present time in Canada we have an alarmingly high rate of mental and social disease. We have an alarmingly high infant mortality rate and very high maternity death rate. We lag far behind New Zealand, Australia and the Scandinavian countries in combating these things. Granting that some part of this situation is due to the fact that we are such an isolated people and that we are not as accessible to doctors and hospitals as are the people in more congested countries, the fact remains that it is futile for us to talk about setting up a sports ministry when at the present time we are unable to provide medical service for large sections of our people, and while we are unable to give proper maternity care or proper pre-natal and postnatal care to thousands of children born in this country. In the province of Saskatchewan a survey was made of several municipalities, in which it was found that thirty-eight per cent of the children in the rural schools had permanent teeth in a state of decay. Last night it was said that this is a task belonging

Public Health-Mr. Pelletier
to the provincial governments. I would agree with the last speaker, who said that the provincial governments and the municipalities can no longer carry that load.
This is what it means: At the present time our health program is very spasmodic. Here you have two municipalities side by side. Through no fault of the residents of those municipalities the financial situation of both is very different. In one municipality they are in a position to take care of the children in their rural schools who need1 dental care or who require their tonsils removed; that work is done for a lump sum. That has been done in a number of well fixed municipalities in Saskatchewan. But in other municipalities whose credit is not so good and where the tax collections have been low, that cannot be done. If we have any money to spend for a sports ministry; if we have any money to spend in looking after the health of the people of Canada, let us spend it in setting up dental clinics, baby clinics and maternity clinics to look after the health of our people.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that any money so spent would be the best investment this parliament ever made. Preventive medicine in any form is not a wasteful extravagance; it is an investment, and a good one. A few years ago it was my privilege to present a brief concerning certain areas in Saskatchewan and to make a study of subnormal families. Without wearying the house let me give just one instance dealing with twelve subnormal families living in one particular locality which, within one generation, produced over two hundred offspring, 178 of whom are still living. Thirty-six per cent of them never reached grade six in school. Thirty-eight per cent suffered from social disease and forty-six per cent live either in penal or in mental institutions. Where formerly there were twelve families living on public charity to-day forty-eight families are living on public charity. The cost of supporting these people has increased fourfold in twenty-five years to say nothing of the moral and physical effect on the remainder of the community as a result of social disease, which they spread very largely.
Any money that may be spent in meeting a problem such as this will be money well invested. In the province of Ontario we have a splendid example of what happens when you have proper medical care applied to children. The Dionne quintuplets have become the wards of the Ontario government'-I assume in view of the fact that the premier of this province has no issue of his own. The care given them has resulted, despite the initial
handicaps, in the raising of five healthy and pretty children. That same care is the birthright of every child born in the Dominion of Canada, whether it be born in a rich home or in a shack on the prairies.
While we in this group therefore are much in favour of recreation and sport in any shape or form, the position we take is that any money this government can afford to spend ought to be spent in looking after our people and in the promotion of preventive medicine.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to take part in this debate for two reasons. At the outset may I say that I have listened very carefully to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), which caused me to look at the resolution once more. I find that the resolution suggests that in the interests of public health a ministry of sports should be established.
I do not believe it is the intention of the mover of this resolution to minimize the value of public health in Canada. Rather by this resolution he attempts to say that, through sports, at least a part of the problem of our national health may be solved. The resolution does not preclude any other attempts being made, through preventive medicine, dental clinics and so on, to meet other branches of the same problem. This is simply advanced as one way to deal with one part of the question. However, I desire to associate myself with the mover of this resolution, because I believe in it in principle. I cannot say that I agree that a ministry of sports should be set up, but I believe the problem is of national importance and for that reason I associate myself with the principle of the resolution.
A second reason why I speak to this motion is that whenever competitive sport is mentioned we naturally think of champions, and, speaking of champions, I come from a province which has produced the greatest champions Canada has ever had, namely the Edmonton Grads. That team needs no introduction in Canada. They are an organization of young ladies known in connection with basketball the world over. Ever since they first won the world's basketball championship they have retained it throughout the years and met all comers, teams from Canada, the United States and Europe, and carried Canada's name to glory wherever they have been. I mention this example because I believe that no debate on sports in this house would be complete without some mention being made of that team. If we inquire into the reasons for their success we shall find that
Public Health-Mr. Power

it is largely due to the systematic methods adopted by their coach. Ever since Percy Page took charge he has been able to turn out champions and keep them champions, something that has never happened before in Canadian sports history. If Canada should decide to supervise in somewhat the same manner but perhaps on a larger and more extensive scale the activities of various sporting organizations, I am sure she would have reason to be proud of the champions she could turn out.
In conclusion may I state once more the views of our group. In principle we agree that there should be some supervision over Canadian sports. We also agree with the hon. member for Weyburn when he says that there are many other improvements to be effected in Canada before making such an attempt as this. The resolution is simply one means of promoting public health and does not preclude any other endeavour of that sort which might be made.

Perhaps I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to say a very few words. Representing as I do the county of Wentworth and part of the city of Hamilton, and coming from a district which has always been held- in rather high regard in the realm of amateur sport in this country, regardless of the fact that the Hamilton Tigers went down to defeat this fall before the Ottawa Rough Riders, and our Dundas Intermediates were defeated by the hon. member for Lambton West's Intermediates-coming as I say from that district I feel bound to express my appreciation of what amateur sport has done and is doing for the youth of this country. I know of no better influence for good in any community than clean, well regulated amateur sport. I am pleased to support more or less the views of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plax-ton). I could not have supported a ministry of sports, but I do congratulate him upon bringing this matter before the house, and I feel it should have the sympathetic consideration of all hon. members.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I desire to thank the mover of the resolution (Mr. Plaxton) for having brought this very important matter to the attention of the people of Canada. There is no doubt whatsoever in my mind that sport, not so much on account of the physical development which results from it as on account of the spirit and mentality which it develops, is of much value to the people of Canada. I am somewhat at a loss, however, to know just- what is meant by the
lMr. Pelletier.]
terms of the resolution. If the hon. gentleman means physical culture in schools, if he means that we should establish a ministry or commission of sports such as they have in Europe, whereby the children are taught physical culture-and perhaps he will not take it amiss if I say are trained to become cannon fodder-then I do not think he is speaking the mind of the people of this country. If on the other hand he means by sports what I shall describe as competitive field sports, such as hockey, football, lacrosse and so on. then I doubt very much whether any nation reared and strengthened on individual effort as Canada has been from the time of our pioneer forefathers, requires any governmental or governing body to teach the youth of this country whether they should or should not play hockey, football or lacrosse.
Hear, hear.

Owing to certain unfortunate occurrences at the last Olympic games an agitation arose to the effect that there should be in Canada some body to decide who should be an amateur and who should be a professional. In my youth, long before I knew anything about this house, I took part in the sports of the day, and in those days there was a definition of amateur and professional. In Canada for a certain period of time those who accepted money for their prowess in athletics were permitted to play with and against those who did not so accept money, as is the case in England to-day in cricket. I think any of my hon. friends who turn to the sports pages in the English papers will see that in the county games Mr. Smith is mentioned, and A. B. Jones, which indicates that one is an amateur and the other a professional.

Whether that is a good system or not I am not prepared to say. But I doubt very much whether it would be in the interests of Canada to say there shall be a minister-who after all originally was a politician'-who shall decide whether or not

Public Health-Mr. Wilton
three members of a team from western Canada sending a challenge in football are professionals. As the person upon whom this task would probably fall, I must say that I would very much like somebody else to undertake it.
Perhaps in this country we have neglected the physical side of education, possibly to our detriment. In so far as my knowledge of constitutional history goes, I understand that this matter would not be within the purview of the federal government. At the present time we have such organizations as the boy scouts and the cadet movements which are carrying on work conducive to the better physical development of the youth of our country. As far as field sports are concerned, as I said, I would not want to be the minister connected therewith. I would not want to be the man who had to choose the referees in the play-offs for the Stanley cup games; I would not want to have to judge horse racing or to see that wrestling matches were not framed in advance. I would not want to be obliged to listen to the tales of prowess related after the nineteenth hole in golf. I feel that the time will come, as it has come in other countries, where the appropriate authority-I do not think this would be the federal authority-will see to it that our children are trained in such a way as to make them strong and healthy in future life and a credit to their race and country. We used to call it physical torture when I was a youth.
The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plax-ton) was kind enough to give me notice of this resolution. I know he spent a great deal of time in preparing his remarks and he even took the trouble to propose a bill. No one in this house has brought more credit to Canada through athletic feats than has the hon. member for Trinity. As a matter of what I would call practical politics or practical administration, I do not think a ministry of sports could be established, whether it were intended for the development of physical culture or for the development of field sports. If my hon. friend will listen to the advice of one who has been somewhat longer in the house than he has, he will withdraw his resolution. He has attained the object which I know he hoped to attain, that of drawing the attention of the people to the fact that the time has come when we must develop our children into healthy men and women.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few words to what has been said already. I am strongly in favour of anything that will
benefit the youth of Canada, representing as I do a city which has produced more amateur champions, both Canadian and world wide, in proportion to its size than any other city in Canada. One of the problems which faces the civic authorities of Hamilton is that of the provision of finances to maintain the public playgrounds. The medical health officer of Hamilton-I believe the same applies to the medical health officers of many other cities-has gone on record as saying that the civic controlled playgrounds are of great advantage in improving the morals and health of the youth of the city. I believe Hamilton was one of the first cities to provide public playgrounds; it led the way in this as it has led the way in many other things. I could give the house a list of thirty or forty outstanding things which have tended to make the world a better place and which had their inception in the city of Hamilton. This city is of so much importance and is so jealously regarded that for some reason it was left out of the official book issued last year by the publicity department at Ottawa and distributed throughout the United States.
Reverting to the matter of playgrounds: a couple of years ago the municipality of Hamilton found itself forced to close some of the playgrounds because of a shortage of funds. It was realized that this would be detrimental to the youth of Hamilton, but it had to be done in the interests of the taxpayers. While I cannot see eye to eye with the mover of the resolution (Mr. Plaxton) when he states that a ministry of sports should be established, I do feel that the government should endeavour to give some financial assistance to municipalities which are conducting public playgrounds. The government would then be doing something which would be greatly in the interests of the health of the youth of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, like other members of the house, I am grateful to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) for introducing this resolution and I feel I would be remiss in my duty to my constituency if I did not make a statement on this occasion.
Every hon. member who has spoken so far has told the house of the number of champions in their respective home towns. We have so many in my county that we take that as a matter of course and keep no record. It is not my intention to spread on the pages of Hansard the names of these ladies and gentlemen who have performed so creditably in the past.

Public Health-Mr. Mallette
In the county of Jacques-Cartier I think we have more golf clubs to the square mile than in any other part of Canada. There is the Royal Montreal Golf Club, the Beacons-field Golf Club, the Marlborough Golf Club, the Beaurepaire Golf Club, the Senneville Golf Club, Elm Ridge Golf Club, Summerlea Golf Club, Grove Hill Golf Club and the Meadowbrook Golf Club, and so on and so forth. If the government were to take over the direction of sports, well, Mr. Speaker, I have enough trouble with patronage as it is without having to put in recommendations for caretakers, for professionals, and perhaps for chamber-maids.
Like the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), when I was young, much younger than now, naturally I used to go in for sports. I was interested in hockey and lacrosse, and when I got older I did what the hon. member for Fort William advised this house to do, I joined a curling club. Not only did I play the game on the ice but I even had something to do with the management of the club, until at last I rose to occupy the very high position of president of the Pointe Claire Curling Club, which is a member of the Canadian branch of the Royal Caledonian Curling Club, an aggregation comprising over 3,300 amateurs in curling in the eastern part of Canada. After a while they elected me president of the Canadian branch of the Royal Caledonian Curling Club. I was informed by the representative of the branch at Montreal that he had written to the secretary of the club in Scotland to tell him that since the foundation of the branch in Montreal in 1852 I was the first French-Canadian to be elected to such high office. This was very satisfactory, but my pride was lowered by the fact that the secretary after five weeks had not answered that communication, and I said that the probable explanation was that he had not yet recovered from the shock.
We have also in Jacques-Cartier race tracks, yacht clubs, boat clubs, canoe clubs, polo clubs, baseball clubs, hockey clubs, in fact, every kind of sport.
I do hope that the government will keep away from sports as much as possible. I know the trouble I would have in my own county well enough not to wish to see members representing other metropolitan counties in similar trouble.
As regards public skating rinks, playgrounds and that kind of thing, in most of the small towns we have them to-day. They are there, and they are provided by the municipal
rMr. Mallette.]
authorities. We did not have such conveniences a generation ago, and where we did have them, it was the boys of those days who had to provide them through their own work and out of their own little savings. But to-day, every time a group wants something it goes to the municipal council, and public moneys must be expended to provide these things. Once you go to the municipal councils, the next move will be to the legislature, and then to the federal government, and if the government undertook to go into this kind of thing we would be asked for grants of all kinds. So I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Trinity will withdraw his resolution. I have just one word to say in appreciation of it, and that is, if the government does go in for controlling sports, that they may take steps to control beauty contests in case another one is held on this hill this year.

In view, Mr. Speaker, of the suggestion made by the hon. Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power), with which I agree, I would ask leave to withdraw my motion.
Motion withdrawn.

subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the Canadian government should consider the advisability of beginning this year to issue purchasing power, and to use that purchasing power for the improvement of the economic condition of the Canadian people.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, before proceeding
to discuss this very vital question I should like to read to the house an excerpt from the introduction to Professor Irving Fisher's book 100% Money, written by Robert H. Hemphill, former credit manager for the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta. In this introduction, among other things he says:
If your personal difficulty and that of all the people you know or know of is lack of money, is it not obvious that the central national difficulty is but the aggregate of, the difficulties of all its citizens, that the scarcity of money is our paramount national problem.
Perhaps I should say something about that before going into my discussion, inasmuch as I know that there are a good many people in this dominion who are trying to draw the attention of the people of Canada from this

Purchasing Power-Mr. Blackmore
question of money, and who are saying there never was more money in the dominion than there is to-day. I grant that fully; but that money is to-day in the hands of men who propose to keep it, and so the ordinary people of Canada are unable to get at it by any means at their command.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I should like to define for the house the term purchasing power. There are two kinds of money. Perhaps a good many people have not come to realize this. There is first what may be called pocket-book money, which consists of coins and bills which you can get hold of-tangible money. This is created generally by governments and by certain banks. Then there is what is known as cheque-book money, or what we might call such. This money is bank credit, and it is created by certain banks. It is really figures in a book. It is utterly intangible, but it is as good as gold, that is, it performs all the functions of any kind of money that can be conceived of, even if that money were pure gold itself. And it is made by the flourish of a fountain pen. I know there will be some who will hasten to challenge that statement, but before they rush in where wiser men may fear to tread may I suggest that they read with considerable care H. D. Macleod's book, Elements of Banking, and especially read page 157. This will show quite clearly that as long ago as 1885 it was fully recognized that there were two distinct kinds of money, that the bankers' cheque-book money is created by the flourish of a fountain pen and is destroyed by the same process; and therein lies a tremendous percentage of the trouble that is to-day afflicting the world. There may be those who will smile at this now, but within twenty years everyone in this dominion who knows anything will recognize it fully and will realize that it is a primary condition to which we should be giving our attention, and for this reason if for no other, that from ninety-five to ninety-seven percent of all the business done in the world to-day, and especially in the Anglo-Saxon world, is done, not with money which you can hold in your hand, but with money represented by figures in a book, transferable by cheque, existing only on the books of the bank. This resolution calls for figures-in-a-book money, for credit, for cheque-book money. A certain amount of pocket-book money also could be issued.
There will be those who will rise and point with gusto to the German mark and to the greenbacks as examples of the colossal failure of this kind of money. Before we waste any time on this sort of thing, let me warn those people that the kind of money I am advocating
has not been used, so far as I have learned, by any government up to the present time. The money I refer to is this credit money or cheque-book money, and the proposal is that the government of the dominion prepare itself, by establishing the necessary machinery and passing the necessary laws, to issue this kind of money and use it. What might easily cause inflation of the regular pocket-book money might be far from having the same effect with cheque-book money, which is figures in a book. At the same time I cannot see that the issue of a certain additional amount of actual pocket-book money could do any harm.
There are a number of urgent reasons why we should begin to issue such money as this. In the first place we are gravely concerned with the national debt. How Canada's national debt can ever be paid off I think we can safely challenge and defy any man in the dominion to-day to show. That debt is increasing, and if we have another war, or if we have to make elaborate preparations for one, our debt can easily assume overwhelming proportions. At the same time that we are worrying about our debt and the paying off of that debt-which we should be worrying about-there are arising in this country from one end to the other demands that more and more consideration shall be given by the government to supporting, financially, various sections of the population. We are to-day about to consider the question of pensions for the blind. Everyone agrees that that is a right principle. Everyone admits that the blind should be supported to such an extent that they can exist comfortably. How much of a burden that will impose upon the dominion government perhaps we should all hesitate to compute. At the same time we are beginning to feel that those who have fought life's battles and who have attained the age of fifty-five or sixty should be allowed to retire to a well-earned rest; and in our economic and industrial conditions to-day the employers are rapidly getting to the point where they force men to take a rest. There are certain industries which have no use for men over forty or forty-five years of age, especially if they are seeking employment for the first time. The problem is not an imaginary one; it is real, and it must be dealt with. How are we going to find the money for the support of such people? As sure as we are in this house, the demand for such support is going to increase.
Besides, as was brought out last night, we must face increasing demands for the support of our burnt-out soldiers; and everyone in
128	COMMONS
Purchasing Power-Mr. Blackmore
this dominion who has a heart realizes that that demand ought to be met, so that the men who fought the battles of this country in the last terrible conflict shall not be obliged to walk down the street as the most shabbily dressed and the most hopeless people in the community. We are being called on constantly, as we have had indicated here to-day, for grants of various kinds. For example, who is there who will argue to-day that the state ought not to consider seriously the question of state medicine and state dental care and state hospitalization? Everyone feels that these things ought to become a reality. Where is the money to come from? And, there are great public works which should be attended to. Our hills are becoming denuded of the virgin forests upon which we depended for the water supply to fill our lakes and supply our rivers. In Alberta this year, and in the west generally, when the drought was upon us, many and many a community was very much at a loss to know what to do to assure itself of a water supply, and that largely because the timber had been removed from the hills which should have been a natural reservoir supplying the streams to give water to those communities. That condition is getting worse. It has been mentioned several times in this parliament.
There should be a reforestation program in this country, but where is the money coming from? Then, everyone realizes that our parks need more and more attention. There is the matter of relief for the unemployed. As far as I can see, this demand will be persistent and perpetual as long as we continue as a nation. Also there is relief for the underpaid. There are some men and some newspapers in this land who sneer because, they say, certain people are receiving more while on relief than they could get if they were working, with the result that some are leaving their work and going on relief. Can you blame them? I do not know of any community in this nation that is giving men more by way of relief than they feel they ought to have; and I maintain that if there are any industries in this country that are giving their employees less than they ought to have, it is a reflection upon this parliament. The indications are that before long something must be done either to force those industries to pay men a living wage or to aid them in supplementing the wages which the men are receiving. How we are to avoid such alarming labour disturbances as are taking place in the United States unless something like that is introduced, I will challenge any man in this dominion to show.

Further than that, the taxation burden, as has already been mentioned several times, has risen to a point at which it can no longer be borne. Something must be done, yet our need for money is more urgent than ever. Can anyone see a way out of that difficulty? There is also the national debt, of which we have been speaking. Some day we must pay that off; we should be starting now. Could we not use the national purchasing power, if we can learn how to use it, so that repayment will not cause any disastrous results? Can we not use it in purchasing the gold which we are producing in this country, the nickel we are producing, and a great number of other commodities, and, with them, help to pay off the national debt? We must find some way of paying it off. How can we do it under the present system?
There is another matter which to my mind is important. Men who are studying these subjects carefully are beginning to learn a great deal about the relation between money in circulation in a country and the income which the people in that country can earn. Robert H. Hemphill, whom I quoted a while ago, has made this statement, that it has been discovered in the United States that for every three dollars which the people of the United States earn as wages, salaries or dividends, there absolutely must be in circulation in that country one dollar. This thing is receiving a scientific approach; men are learning that certain monetary laws must be regarded. If at the present time we cannot devise a method of getting money into circulation by means which we have thus far used, then unquestionably we must find some other way of getting that money into circulation. There is simply no use in our closing our eyes to that fact.
Then, in addition there is the matter of increasing our production. Production increases according to the amount of money we have in circulation. That is a fact which some people may not realize, but one which is nevertheless true. At the present time banks cannot give enough money to increase production as we would have it increased.

speechtext:
I am pleased the
minister has asked the question. I wish to deal with it, because there is no doubt that those factors are vitally bound up. In order to increase production of a hundred acres of wheat or a hundred sheep under present circumstances a man must be in a position to borrow money, unless he happens to have it in his own account. If he has it, then when he invests the money in the sheep he looks upon that money as a debt which, together with interest, must be paid back to him, so that it may pay him to invest money in the sheep rather than put the sum into the bank. If he cannot get the money and the interest back, he will not invest the money. So in a very real way it might be said that every dollar we are using to-day goes out into circulation as a debt.
There will be those who may challenge my statement, and when they do I shall be pleased to answer them, because I have plenty of authority with which to meet the challenge. Our money is all debt. As one notable authority I quote Robert H. Hemphill, a man who I presume ought to know a good deal about these things, as he holds the position of manager of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta. These are his words as they appear in a foreword to Irving Fisher's book 100% Money:
If all bank loans were paid no one would have a bank deposit,-
In the press of Canada and in after-dinner speeches we hear a great deal about deposits. May I say the people of our country must learn much more about the nature of deposits. I repeat the quotation:
If all bank loans were paid no one would have a bank deposit, and there would not be a dollar of currency or coin in circulation.
This is a staggering thought. We are completely dependent on the commercial banks. Someone has to borrow every dollar we have in circulation, cash or credit. If the banks create ample synthetic money we are prosperous; if not, we starve. We are absolutely without a permanent monetary system. When one gets a complete grasp upon this picture, the tragic absurdity of our helpless position is almost incredible. But there it is.
Why cannot the banks issue enough money? Simply because the banker cannot issue money unless he has a borrower; of the borrowers presenting themselves to banks for loans only 31111-9
a few can be trusted by the banker, and most of those whom the banker can trust will not trust themselves. The result is that they do not borrow. There is enough evidence to prove that beyond the shadow of a doubt.
There will be those who will say there is more money on deposit in the banks to-day than there was in 1929. Yes, that is true; but what is that money on deposit? The money on deposit is largely loans which the bankers have advanced to governments. That is an important point to remember. The money in question is not therefore out in circulation as we might be led to believe; it is already tied up.
More and more of bank loans are being advanced to governments and consequently are not in circulation. This is a very serious matter. Then, money must be in circulation to decrease unemployment. If money is not in circulation, men are not able to get it and are therefore unable to buy the goods industry produces. As a result, industries are not in a position to run full time; consequently they are unable to employ men full time. If we are to get employment for our people we must find some way of getting them back to work, and we cannot get them back to work until we can create payment for our goods.
It is said that we will do that through international trade.	Perhaps-but the best
thinkers I find have not much faith in international trade as a solution for all our problems. The cause of the depression is financial, although many people will doubt that statement. I repeat that beyond all question the cause of the depression is financial, and money must be put into circulation to bring us out of it. If we had some means of producing national money we could increase our defence without inflicting undue burden upon Canada. This country can produce practically everything necessary to equip itself with almost any degree of defence it may wish. Why can we not produce the goods and equip ourselves for defence measures?
Then, there is a still more serious matter to consider-and again there will be hon. members in the house who will challenge what I am about to say. I am positive, so far as I have been able to get information, that there is no successful answer to the statement that the government of Canada and of virtually every modern country is controlled by financial institutions. Consequently democracy is passing away. Yesterday the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) talked about the way in which democracy has failed. I believe I have indicated
