one good and sufficient reason why it is failing, and unless we can change tihis matter of the control of money I say democracy will continue to fail. There is a reason why Germany has gone fascist; there is a reason why Italy has done likewise; there is a reason why Russia has gone communist.
Then, having established the need for such money, if we can find a way in which to get it, the next question is this:	Is such money
feasible? Is it practicable to have national money, and particularly national credit? There are three main questions which arise in discussing this matter. First, could Canada have the power to create national money? I believe we need not discuss that question, but we shall at a later time glance at it from two or three aspects. Second, should national money be sound money? The expression "sound money" has gone back and forth from one end of this country to the other, and we are led to ask ourselves:	What is sound
money?

The laugh will be on the other side of the faces before long, too. All right; think of an island like Ontario, filled with natural riches. Could that island have money? If the government of the island created money, what would be the backing of that money? For those who are so exceedingly smart over there let me suggest that they go and get Sir Norman

Purchasing Power-Mr. Blackmore
Angell's series of articles which appeared in the Financial Post last year. Read them through with a great deal of care; turn to page 19 and read this little illustration, and see what you get out of it. I am going to retell it now. He says a sailor landed on a certain island with a block of gold. He wanted to use the gold in order to buy certain goods for his own use, but at the time he did not see how he could use the gold. So he went to a missionary and confided the gold to his keeping, saying, "As soon as you get a chance, take my gold to the old country and have it minted. Meanwhile I will write orders against it." So the sailor wrote orders and passed them to the natives in return for the goods which the natives gave him. In due time the natives were passing a great quantity of these orders around the island, and accepting them as face value as money. But, Sir Norman Angell says, the gold never did go to the old country; it never was minted into coin, but the system continued to function just the same, and the gold might just as well have been a piece of lead. When hon. gentlemen opposite get through explaining that it will be plenty of time to sneer. Until they can explain it, however, they would be wise not to reveal their ignorance; until they can explain that away it might be just as well to keep right on studying.
Now, the question is, what was the backing of the money when it was in circulation in the island?

speechtext: Very good, but you will find that the backing of that money was the goods and services, the producing and consuming power of that island, the exchanges, as Sir Norman Angell says. It will take a good deal of laughing to explain that away.

speechtext: Nor anything like it.

speechtext:
Get the pamphlet; read page 19, and we will see. At any rate, this is an illustration.
What is the backing of money? That is the question. The backing of money is the goods and services, the producing and consuming power of a country; in other words, the need of the country for the money. What do authorities say about it? In 1936 Senator Owen wrote an article which completely supports that stand; in 1936 Reginald Mac-Kenna made a statement completely supporting that stand, as far as I can see. On January 30, 1936, he is credited with having uttered these words:
Additional currency, however, can now be furnished by the authorities, if they choose to exercise their powers, without reference to the central bank's holdings of gold. Thus the nineteenth century, which brought into general use a means of payment hitherto scarcely known outside London-
He is referring there to the power of creating credit and transferring it by cheque. -brought also the machinery whereby it could be subjected to intelligent control.
In his 100% Money, Irving Fisher supports the same idea time and again. Then G. D. H. Cole, eminent Oxford economist, has; written the following words in his Principles of Economic Planning, at page 213:
Whenever the need arises to increase the supply of money, I am suggesting that the increase ought to be made, not in the form of increased loan credits to either producers or consumers, but of non-repayable presents of purchasing power to all the citizens, save to the extent to which the state decides to use the money itself for public purposes.
And at page 217 we find these words:
It does seem to me undeniable that the state, by creating new money without thereby creating new debt, can come near to bringing about the full use of the available productive resources, and can, by recurrent infusions of additional money, keep those resources in use.
Those who talk about the dangers of inflation must remember that they are challenging the words of a man who stands very high in the economic life of Great Britain. Here is another quotation, from page 208:
Let the state, it is urged, create more purchasing power, and more production will speedily follow.
This will answer the question proposed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). Again:
I do not dispute this. I agree that, if the state makes a present of new money to consumers-not a credit advance, repayable later on, but a present-the effect will be to stimulate additional production.

Purchasing Poiver-Mr. Blackmore
There are many more statements that I could read. The question is, What is the backing of money? There are books written to show that the gold standard has broken down, that the backing of money is no longer gold, and the wisest men know it is not. Nor is the backing any other metal. It is the goods and services, and the producing and consuming power of the community, and the credit and confidence the people have-

He is the chairman of the monetary reform committee of the United States. I am sorry the hon. member does not know. He says:
There is no mystery in what makes the value of money,

speechtext: These are nearly all foreign authorities. The hon. member passes over those of his own province.

subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: If you would leave the province alone it might do better. The value of money depends absolutely upon the supply of money in relation to the demand for money, entirely regardless of the value of gold content.

subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: What creates the demand for money ?

subtopic: PROPOSED CREATION AND ISSUE OF NATIONAL CREDIT FOR IMPROVEMENT OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
The desire of the people to produce, motivated by their desire to consume, operating through effective demand.
Then the next point, Would such money cause inflation? First, what is inflation? We say ordinarily that inflation means a fall in the purchasing power of a dollar or rise in the price of commodities in terms of that dollar. You will all agree with that, I think. But another definition of inflation we cannot allow. It is the definition which has been used by a great many propagandists throughout the country, who contend that any kind of money created by anybody but a banker is inflation. This is an absolute lie.

The next question is, What is the cause of inflation? The main cause of inflation is having too much money in circulation actually among the people for the goods and services that are available. That is the test. More money gradually introduced into circulation will cause more production, as was brought out a few minutes ago in Senator Owen's article, giving more backing for more money Our ability to produce goods and services is almost unlimited. Of that there is no question, otherwise why all the unemployment and all the half-time work? What do the authorities say about this matter? Let me read a passage from Paul Einzig's book World Finance Since 1914, published in 1935, page 17:
The more advanced definitions-
That is of inflation.
-duly allow for any change in the volume of real wealth. Thus if the volume of currency and credit increases, and the production of real wealth increases in the same proportion, then there is no reason why the expansion of currency and credit should produce an inflationary effect, even if it affects the spending power of the community. It is only if the increase of currency and credit is in excess of the additional production of real wealth that it is defined as being of inflationary character.
That, I think admits of no successful contradiction.
The next question is, What about our present system? Our present system is the system that causes inflation, and the people who cause the inflation are the very ones who are everlastingly telling us that the government issue of money would cause inflation. You will find that in the platforms of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the United States, and the same thing applies to us, that it is the indefensible expansion and contraction of credit that causes the trouble. Anyone who wants a good discussion of this should read Irving Fisher's 100% Money, after which I will talk with him privately. For the United States Professor Fisher uses these figures, and I think corresponding figures can be found for Canada. In the United States in 1926 there were four billions of pocketbook money in circulation, and twenty-two billions of cheque book money. Between 1926 and 1929 the amount of pocketbook money remained the same, but the cheque book money increased from twenty-two to twenty-three billions, and Professor Fisher says definitely that that increase of one billion of cheque book money caused the inflation and the subsequent collapse which resulted in this disastrous depression. In 1933 there were five billions of pocketbook money,

Purchasing Power-Mr. Deachman
because President Hoover, in an attempt to change the situation had introduced one billion more, but there were only fifteen billions of cheque book money. And that is what caused the depression and is continuing it.
Now may I read a passage which is rather enlightening, from Professor Fisher's book "100% Money", page 6 of his summary:
An essential part of this depression has been the shrinkage from the 23 to the 15 billions in cheque book money, that is, the wiping-out of 8 billions of dollars of the nation's chief circulating medium which we all need as a common highway for business.
This loss, or destruction, of 8 billions of cheque book money has been realized by few and seldom mentioned.

There would have been big newspaper headlines if 8 thousand miles out of 23 thousand miles of railway had been destroyed. Yet such a disaster would have been a small one compared with the destruction of 8 billions out of 23 billions of our main monetary highway. That destruction of 8 billion dollars of what the public counted on as their money was the chief sinister fact in the depression from which followed the two chief tragedies, unemployment and bankruptcies.
If that writer knows what he is talking about can there be any question as to the cause of the depression?
In closing I submit that inasmuch as the present system presents to us only despair and failure, inasmuch as there is grave need of new money without debt and without taxation, inasmuch as the thoughts of a great many progressive men are leading them to the conclusion that national money is the way out, inasmuch as national money is sound and constitutional and safe, or could be, and could be and should be abundant, inasmuch as the national credit has never been tried and consequently no one knows whether it would cause inflation or not, and inasmuch as national credit ought to work, for 97 per cent of business is now done on credit, I urge the government to consider very seriously the matter of the creation of new purchasing power.

speechtext:
Speaking in the house a few days ago the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) made an appeal to the members for sympathy in regard to conditions existing in western Canada. I am quite sure that appeal will be met almost without being made. We in the House of Commons to-day owe a great debt to the people of western Canada. I would point out that at the present moment there are five political groups in this house. Every one of the leaders of these distinct groups represents a constituency in western Canada. In addition to that we have three provincial ex-premiers. Surely, as far as western Canada is concerned we have sufficient leading in the dominion at the present time. What we need, in order to accomplish the desired end, is just a little more light. I appeal to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, and to his friends, to give us a clearer explanation of what they really intend to do. I listened to my hon. friend this afternoon as closely as I could. He told) us of the things that ought to be done, but he did not utter a single word of detail.
He asks for an increase of purchasing power. Purchasing power is something which must be created, not given, if a nation is going to prosper. My hon. friend talks about an island. I do not like his island, it is too large. It is almost as large as the province of Ontario and it does not suit my purpose at the moment. Will hon. members permit me to take them to another island, a nice productive island, large enough to accommodate every hon. member in the house and perhaps some of those who assist us in the work we do here? This is a fertile island and all that is required to bring forth fruit is labour. I ask my hon. friend a question, the answer to which can come during the session from him or from some other member of his group: What will be the purchasing power of my hon. friend when he is settled upon that island? What will be his purchasing power at the end of his first year upon the island? I tell the house what I think his answer will be. His purchasing power will be measured exactly by his production.
Every hon. member on that island will bring to the market place the products which he has produced. His capacity to buy or to purchase the goods which others have produced will be determined by the volume and value of the products which he brings to the market place. In time a price system will evolve which will establish the relative price relationships between different products. Not everyone will produce grain or fruit. Perhaps some will make speeches. Some will be civil servants and perhaps we may have a governor on that island. It may be desirable to have some music. I would be willing to make a contribution in order that

Purchasing Power-Mr. Deachman______
the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) might be present. I submit that the purchasing power of that island will depend upon production and there is no other way in which you can increase it.
Then the hon. member for Lethbridge comes upon the scene and says, "We ought to increase the purchasing power." How can you do it? You can do it only by taking from some who have produced and giving it to others. There may be some increase in consuming power through exchange with the other islands which surround you, but the ultimate standard of living on that island will depend upon the productive power of the island and upon the exchanges which take place with the other surrounding islands. I ask my hon. friend to think over this matter very carefully.
I ask my hon. friend and his friends to change, in their imaginations, this island into the province of Alberta. Exactly the same conditions prevail. Will it make any difference how often you change your government in the province of Alberta? Will it help you if you bring out money with stamps on the back of it? Will it help you if you put in a double or triple system of currency? Is there any means by which your consumptive power can be increased except by production, plus favourable exchange? I think my hon. friends ought to give an answer to that question. If they do not give an answer, then I think they ought to try to present to us what they deem to be an answer.^ We should be given an opportunity to examine it.
I read the platform of the Aberhart party -I cannot call it the social credit party because it certainly is not that-in the papers a few days ago. Its planks have been brought up again by the hon. member for Lethbridge. What does he say? He says that we should have an issue of debt free money. I should like to know what constitutes debt free money. If I am a farmer in Alberta and want to borrow $500 with which to purchase twenty steers at $25 each in order that I may feed them on my land, can I, under the system proposed by my hon. friend, go to the government and ask for $500? When that is done, can I say to myself that I hold in my hand $500 which I have received from the Alberta government and which will purchase for me twenty steers? Can I say that I have no obligation to pay that back and that I have no obligation to pay interest upon it? If that be true, the government of Alberta could give me the twenty steers. It could give me machinery and equipment to any amount, and there
(Mr. Deachman.]
would be no interest to pay. Houdini on the stage took rabbits out of his hat'-Houdini could not make his living by selling the rabbits. Yet that is the proposal made by my hon. friend.
I do not want to continue the argument to any great length, but I warn my hon. friend that I shall stay here as long as he and Mr. Aberhart survive. I only want him and those who support him to tell us how they will increase purchasing power. I want to know what he will do about debt free money. I want to know how long he will continue to issue debt free money. I want him to face the simplest of simple problems. If that could be done in Alberta, would it follow that the government of that province could buy control of the Royalite oil wells by the use of debt free money? I want to know if they could buy control of Noranda mines. I want to know if they could buy up the obligations of another province and live upon the interest. Is there any limitation to this scheme which they propose? Can it be continued indefinitely, or is it to be limited to just such things as we witnessed last summer when for a brief time they issued a few dollars of script money. The only thing they got out of it was a headache, plus the price they received1 for a few souvenirs that were sold. It is not a difficult question that I ask. I simply ask that these gentlemen tell us how it can be done. You cannot prove it by citing the most learned authority, by quoting Norman Angell or anyone else. You must put this system to the test, and unless that can be done it is useless. They have been trying to do it for a long time in Alberta, but so far they have not succeeded. If my hon. friend were given that marvellous gift which he says the bankers hold, would he stop at the paltry $18,000,000 which the banks of Canada earned last year? Any organization with such limitless possibilities for creating wealth could make the Count of Monte Cristo look like a piker? The government of Alberta has been trying these things and all they have left at the present time is the little sheet of paper which I hold in my hand- the outline of things they propose to do in the future. What do we ask for? We ask for a simple plan and a simple statement of fact. You cannot in this world get something for nothing without taking that something away from somebody else-if you can will you tell us how it is to be done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to support this resolution of my leader (Mr. Blackmore). The interest which the dis-

Purchasing Power-Mr. Hayhurst
cussion has provoked in this house is an indication of the very deep concern taken in this vital question all over this dominion. The people of this country at least are recognizing that something must be done to alleviate conditions as they have developed in Canada and other countries.
Our good friend from Huron North (Mr. Deachman) says that you cannot get something for nothing, but surely he does not mean that. Why, some of the best things in life are something for nothing. The rain that falls upon our land, the sunshine that ripens the crop these are something for nothing, and they are vital to production. We in this part of the house hope in our time to disprove some of the fallacies which have been enunciated by the hon. member for Huron North. It is singular that he should still preach the doctrine that production must accompany purchasing power. If he had farmed in western Canada, as most of us here have done, where we produce large quantities of wheat and other cereals, potatoes and other products, he would know that the man who grows a ton of potatoes does not produce the money that will purchase them. We produce goods in enormous quantities, and usually at a loss. If I may be pardoned for making a personal reference, last fall I shipped ten head of pure bred shorthorn cattle, weighing on the average 200 pounds each, and all they brought in the Edmonton market was S6 each, or $3 a hundred pounds. Will anyone in this house say that a man can produce beef at that rate? Beef is one of the real assets of this country, and we cannot continue to produce at that rate when we have no control whatsoever of the value of money. The yield does not furnish the proper equivalent for me to buy my requirements in clothing and food, and that is due to the tremendous cost of production of that real wealth.
The hon. member for Huron North mentioned that wonderful island of his.

speechtext: No, your island.

I will give you the story of another island, where this question of money was considered, and I am going to quote an authority. Mr. A. DeV. Leigh, who is secretary of the London Chamber of Commerce. He has written the story of an island, and I am going to quote it because it illustrates some of the ideas that have been expressed by the hon. member for Huron North:
It is said that on a certain coast long ago shark's teeth were used for money. These answered the purpose all right and the industries of this primitive people were carried on very well with this currency. For years the country was prosperous, but storms ravished a nearby coast along which they had caught their supply of sharks. The storms destroyed the sharks and for a number of years no more could be procured. Money grew scarce in the island; industry languished, and the people became reduced to penury, all because of the scarcity of shark's teeth.
Then sharks became available once more, shark's teeth became plentiful, and the people had money. They went to work again, industry recovered, and the inhabitants of the island regained their former state of comfort. This situation recurred several times in the course of a long period of years, the plight of the people becoming worse each time of scarcity, yet no remedy was found.
A visitor to these shores during one of those seasons of depression was astounded at what he saw-people starving in a land where food was plentiful, for want of shark's teeth. He pointed out to them how ludicrous their attitude was in the eyes of a stranger, and they came to see that another standard than shark's teeth could be used without destroying any of the wealth of the country. At last they understood that the material of which money was made mattered little and that another medium than shark's teeth could be used and the integrity of the money would remain; that it was the relation of their medium of exchange to production which really mattered. Money is for the purpose of exchanging goods so its relation to the production of the country should be sound-[DOT]

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) says "hear, hear," to that. It goes on:
-and any other foundation for money is essentially unsound.
I hope that the discussion which this resolution is provoking in the house will be of value to all the members, and I sincerely hope that many members of the cabinet will take part in the discussion.
I think it was the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) who asked the question: What is the relationship between production and purchasing power? That question probably has not yet been answered. The difficulty, as we see it, is that those who are in control of money do not issue money based upon real wealth but issue it upon some mystical standard, whether it is called the gold standard or by some other name, rather than upon the productive capacity of the country.
What we ask in this resolution is that the government should take power to create its own money based upon its own credit. In our judgment there are two great errors in
136	COMMONS
Purchasing Power-Mr. Hayhurst
our existing economic system. First, incomes are inevitably lower than prices. Second, the government taxes us to pay interest on its credit, instead of creating its own capital money and income money. The amount of money that is paid out as income and is available to buy retail goods for consumption, as distinguished from capital money, can only be used through industry producing new goods, and in turn income money is required to buy those products of industry. The amount of income money thus distributed to the community in a given period of normal trade is less than the total sale prices of all the retail goods finished and put on the market in that period. That is one reason why all retail goods cannot be sold and a million and more producers at times are put out of work, and that is the reason why we pass through periods of depression such as we have been passing through in the last few years, and from which, through the manipulation of currency or credit control, we may escape into another period of more or less so-called prosperity. No dealing out of words can supersede realities, nor can it save the unemployed men from feeling the pinch and the degradation. The fact is there, whatever words we may use. The accumulation of capital in the form of reserves of industrial companies cannot be spent on buying consumption goods, so however huge the balance may be there is no solution to the poverty problem until that balance has been spent on incomes.
In time of war it seems that any nation is able to produce all the money it requires to make armaments. Shells are not sold, but destroyed, so that definitely brings us a little boom, because money is put into circulation for goods which are not bought in a retail market. But alas, the government borrows the money instead of creating it, and when this spurt of armament making is over it will have to collect income money in the form of taxes out of our meagre incomes in order to pay the interest on the sinking fund. More will have to be borrowed in order to help us pay our taxes. Again economists will note the inevitable slump and explain it by spots on the sun instead of advising the government to make new money for whatever expenses are necessary.
There should be no need to tax us to final hopeless poverty, if the money is not borrowed from outside the community. The trouble to-day is that we give too much prestige to

our money market, which is a. poor substitute for our great industries. I ask this question: Which is greater, a nation of usurers, money lenders and barterers, or a nation of producers which can provide all its steel and engineering and electrical equipment? I should judge that a nation of producers is more important than a nation of traders or usurers. As I see it, the fact is that to-day we are using a money system which has been outlived; which was perfectly satisfactory, perhaps, for an age of scarcity, but which, through the technological improvements of modern industry, has not kept pace with the times. The technological improvements of to-day have changed our entire outlook on life. This afternoon we listened to some speeches about sports. Shakespeare used these words:
If all the year weTe playing holidays,
To sport would be as tedious as to work.
To-day the engineers of the world have changed our productive capacity to such an extent that leisure and sport and play will become much more prevalent, because the " grinding necessity " of labour is no longer a necessity. In the production of all goods less economic energy is required, but it should be our object not to restrict and destroy goods, but rather to distribute them, for the object of production should be consumption.
How strange that a young country such as Canada should deliberately stop the admission of desirable elements from abroad solely because they cannot present clear and convincing evidence that they have adequate means of supporting themselves for an indefinite period after their arrival. It happens that my constituency is very largely Ukrainian, and in representing them I had the honour last year of going to the immigration department to endeavour to arrange for the admission from the Ukraine of a number of the sons and daughters of families here who had been separated by immigration officials from their relatives. But it was impossible to get any favourable answer, because we could not prove that if these people came to Canada they would be employed or would have enough money to keep them for some indefinite period of time Thus it is that the monetary conceptions of our government and many of our people are placed in the forefront of their thinking and are more important to them than the real asset of the people of this great dominion. What the dominion lacks more than anything else is people; we have tremendous resources and yet we have the

unemployed. People ask:	Where is the
money coming from to put these unemployed to work? We contend that the money should be issued in proportion to the productive capacity of the men; and if, as someone has said, gold has intrinsic value, it and other metals, as well as wheat and other commodities, could be used for the issuance of credit or money.
